source_meta.title: WHO recommendations for management of serious bacterial infections in infants aged 0-59 days

sections.summary: In non-hospital settings, the WHO 7-sign IMCI algorithm is recommended to identify young infants (0-59 days) with possible serious bacterial infection who need further evaluation or treatment. Strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence, based on two studies (9284 infants) showing sensitivity ~0.79 and specificity ~0.77 overall.
Young infants aged 0-59 days with IMCI signs of critical illness should be referred to hospital. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence (no included trials; based on GDG consensus).

If hospital referral is not possible for an infant with critical illness, ampicillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 10 days is recommended. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence.

Young infants with IMCI signs of clinical severe infection should be referred to hospital. If referral is not possible, oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 7 days is recommended. Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence, based on four trials (9823 infants).

If 7 days of gentamicin IM is not feasible, oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days plus gentamicin IM/IV for only 2 days may be considered. Conditional recommendation, low-certainty evidence, based on a single trial in Africa.

Young infants aged 0-6 days with fast breathing as the only IMCI sign of illness should be referred to hospital. If referral is not possible, oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days is recommended. Strong recommendation, low-certainty evidence, based on two RCTs (1308 infants).

Young infants aged 7-59 days with fast breathing as the only IMCI sign of illness should be treated with oral amoxicillin for at least 7 days and can be managed outside hospital. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence, based on three trials (4307 infants).

No recommendation made on use of hospital-based clinical-sign algorithms for diagnosing sepsis in infants 0-59 days, as all 28 reviewed studies used algorithms with laboratory tests not currently feasible in low-resource settings. Further research proposed using harmonized, standardized assessment tools.

In young infants aged 0-59 days hospitalized with suspected sepsis, ampicillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 10 days is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management. Strong recommendation, moderate-certainty evidence, based on six trials (1083 infants) comparing third-generation cephalosporins to this regimen.

In young infants hospitalized with suspected staphylococcal sepsis, cloxacillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 10 days is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence; no included trials, based on GDG consensus. This is a pathogen-directed regimen (staphylococcal coverage), not treatment of a generic named condition.
unmapped_entities: Staphylococcus species (unspecified - document does not distinguish S. aureus vs coagulase-negative staphylococci)

sections.summary: In young infants hospitalized with suspected meningitis, ampicillin, cefotaxime or ceftriaxone IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least three weeks is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence; no included trials, based on GDG consensus. Ampicillin should be added to third-generation cephalosporin plus gentamicin (triple therapy) specifically when Listeria monocytogenes is suspected -- a pathogen-directed addition rather than treatment of the general condition.

In young infants hospitalized with suspected pneumonia, ampicillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 7 days is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence; no included trials, based on GDG consensus.

In young infants hospitalized with suspected staphylococcal pneumonia, cloxacillin IM/IV plus gentamicin IM/IV for at least 7 days is recommended as first-choice antibiotic management. Strong recommendation, very low-certainty evidence; no included trials. Pathogen-directed regimen (staphylococcal coverage).
